From July 1, 2026, new graduate students in the US can no longer borrow federal Grad PLUS loans; when a program costs more than the federal limits, the rest can come from a private lender. Leah, an illustrative student, has two private offers: 9% fixed, or variable starting lower, at 7.5%. This video replays her illustrative loan, $50,000 over 10 years (120 monthly payments), through every 10-year stretch of US interest rates since January 1954, to see how much lower a variable rate has had to start before the risk was worth it, in history.

"Worth it" has one plain meaning here: how often the variable loan cost more in total interest than the 9% fixed loan, and how much more at worst.

What the replay found (history, not a forecast; US only; ILLUSTRATIVE: Leah's pair of rates and her loan are not a real lender's offer)
- Leah's head start is 1.5 points (9% fixed minus 7.5% variable). At some point her variable rate rose above 9% in 76.2% of stretches, yet it cost more in total interest in 14.2%: 28.4% of starts from 1954 to 1980 and 3.5% of starts from 1981 on. The worst stretch, from April 1977, cost $11,219 more, 43% more interest than the fixed loan's $26,005.
- The best stretch began in August 1981 and cost $15,295 less than the fixed loan.
The same replay with the fixed rate held at 9% and other variable starting rates:
- 3 points: 4.5% of all starts cost more in total interest; 10.5% of starts from 1954 to 1980, none (0%) of starts from 1981 on; the worst stretch (April 1977) cost $6,033 more.
- 2 points: 8.8% of all starts cost more in total interest; 20.4% of starts from 1954 to 1980, none (0%) of starts from 1981 on; the worst stretch (April 1977) cost $9,472 more.
- 1 point: 31.3% of all starts cost more in total interest; 54.9% of starts from 1954 to 1980, 13.5% of starts from 1981 on; the worst stretch (April 1977) cost $12,983 more.
- 0 points: 57.9% of all starts cost more in total interest; 79% of starts from 1954 to 1980, 42% of starts from 1981 on; the worst stretch (April 1977) cost $16,566 more.
- Minus 1 point (the variable rate starts above the fixed rate): 72.9% of all starts cost more in total interest; 92.9% of starts from 1954 to 1980, 57.8% of starts from 1981 on; the worst stretch (April 1977) cost $20,217 more.
- At every head start tested, the worst stretch began in April 1977, and some of the starts from 1954 to 1980 still cost more (at least 10.5%).

How the replay was built (method card)
- A variable rate is a lender's index plus a fixed margin. Here the 3-month Treasury bill rate stands in for the lender's index (3.72% in August 2026), with a margin of 3.78 points, set so that Leah's variable rate starts at 7.5%.
- Each replay moves her rate up and down exactly as much as the Treasury bill rate moved in that stretch of history; the index is never taken below zero.
- 753 start months: the first replay starts in January 1954, then one every month to September 2016; each runs 10 years (120 monthly payments) against 9% fixed.
- Neighbouring stretches overlap, so the 753 starts are not independent tests.
- No grace period, no fees, no rate cap: repayment starts at once, with no deferment and no discounts. A real loan's cap, if low enough, would have made the worst case smaller.
- Every dollar amount is in dollars of the day (nominal, not adjusted for inflation).

What this is and is not
- History, not a forecast. Which kind of history comes next is something no replay can show.
- US only: US Treasury bill rates and US federal student loan rules.
- Not advice. The line does not say which offer is better; it shows what each head start meant in each kind of history. A real offer has its own two rates, its own head start, and what this replay leaves out: the lender's real index, a rate cap, a grace period, fees, and the borrower's own budget.
- ILLUSTRATIVE: Leah, her two rates and her loan are illustrative, not a real lender's offer. The Treasury bill history is real data.

Federal loan context
- From July 1, 2026, new graduate students can no longer borrow federal Grad PLUS loans. Students already enrolled and borrowing before July 2026 keep Grad PLUS for up to 3 more academic years, or for the time left in their program if that is shorter.
- New students still have the Direct Unsubsidized loan: up to $20,500 a year and $100,000 total, with higher limits in professional programs such as medicine or law.
